synopsis: Physics-based and data-driven sensor models form a continuum rather than mutually exclusive alternatives: physics models compute causal responses, while learned models reproduce recorded distributions, and neither has an unconditional advantage [f13087, f4463, f4328, f13096]. Physics-based models can respond to changed machines, materials and sensor positions, making them attractive for a program covering different sensor heights, but transfer of validity across mounting positions was not demonstrated; measured job-site material data are also missing, and heavy precipitation or simplified physics can undermine accuracy [f4466, f13097, f5118, f13098, f4470, f4473]. The recommended division of labor is physics-based testing of important sensor effects and selected corner cases, with learned models supporting training, replay editing, scenario variation and robustness testing; hybrids should anchor important physical dimensions in physics and real measurements, but their maturity for safety credit remains unresolved [f4474, f4491, f4919, f5078]. Reduced-order motion and braking surrogates fitted to high-fidelity simulation and tests are common and very fast, suitable for millions of threshold and uncertainty evaluations, but unsafe extrapolation is a risk and no earth-moving transfer benchmark was found [f6105, f6481, f6482, f6479]. ASME V&V 40-2018 and the November 2023 FDA guidance are rated the most transferable credibility framework, but their stated scope is physics-based models, leaving machine-learned perception needing separate assurance [f8077, f8220]. Practical maturity remains uneven: calibrated construction-vehicle twins existed in 2025 but focused on dynamics and digging rather than perception, physics-based lidar is the most mature sensor family, and physics-based ultrasonic simulation was not found in Isaac Sim, Chrono::Sensor or CARLA [f468, f4501, f8547].
